title: Why should you never scare a vulture?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore vultures: a French hiker's body was picked clean by griffon vultures in about forty-five minutes, which they tie to French protection laws and farmers burning livestock carcasses. They cover Himalayan sky burials and the decline of vultures in India and Nepal due to the veterinary drug diclofenac, which killed Old World species. They discuss vultures' ecological role in breaking disease chains, their acidic digestion, featherless heads, urinating on their legs for cooling and sanitation, defensive vomiting, Old World versus New World vulture differences, group names, and a forensic study using vultures at a Texas State body farm. A listener mail story about a Vancouver bartender and a bachelor party tipping test closes the episode, along with an author plug for Thomas Trask.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about haircuts, fight club, and fish-hook moves, then Josh introduces the topic with the story of a hiker in the Pyrenees whose body was cleaned by vultures within forty-five minutes.

segments.title: French vultures and Himalayan sky burials
segments.summary: The hosts explain that French protections for vultures and farmers burning livestock carcasses left vultures hungry. They then describe Zoroastrian and Tibetan Buddhist sky burials in the Himalayas, which are threatened by the shortage of vultures.

segments.title: Diclofenac and vulture decline
segments.summary: The drug diclofenac, used on cattle, caused kidney failure in vultures that ate treated carcasses, wiping out three Old World species in India. India banned it in 2006, and vulture numbers began rising in 2012. Vultures are described as important for sanitation and disease control.

segments.title: Vulture ecology and species differences
segments.summary: Vultures are described as nature's cleanup crew, breaking disease chains and clearing carcasses quickly. The hosts contrast Old World vultures in the Eastern Hemisphere, which are related to hawks and eagles, with New World vultures in the Western Hemisphere, which are not closely related. They discuss the California condor and the African lappet-faced vulture.

segments.title: Vulture anatomy, smell, and sanitation
segments.summary: The hosts explain that vultures have bald heads for hygiene, have no real song, and rely on keen sight or smell to find carcasses. They describe urinating on their legs to cool down and kill bacteria. They note that vultures have few natural predators.

segments.title: Defensive vomiting and acidic stomach
segments.summary: Vultures vomit when startled, which lightens them for flight and may serve as a decoy; bald eagles eat the vomit. Vulture stomach acid has a pH between one and two, which kills many pathogens such as anthrax spores.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A message break from the show.

segments.title: Forensic use of vultures and paragliding
segments.summary: A Texas State University study used a body at the body farm and recorded vultures on camera, finding that a group of American black vultures cleaned the body in five hours and spread remains over fifteen weeks. The hosts also mention paragliding in the Himalayas with trained vultures.

segments.title: Listener mail: Vancouver bartender tipping test
segments.summary: A Vancouver bartender describes a bachelor party that tested tipping by leaving nickels for days, then leaving a $2,000 envelope on the final day. Josh and Chuck comment on the story and sign off with a plug for Thomas Trask's book Prism.
